validated_results.title: Non-occupational risk factors for bladder cancer: a case-control study.
validated_results.reason: Hospital-based case-control study of newly diagnosed bladder cancer reporting a multivariate-adjusted estimate for pork (red meat) intake by tertile.

extraction.comparison_type: highest versus lowest tertile of pork intake
extraction.population: newly diagnosed bladder cancer patients and individually matched controls

cases.excerpt: A hospital-based, case-control study included 130 newly diagnosed bladder cancer patients and the same number of individually matched controls with respect to sex, age (+/- 2 years) and type of residence (rural or urban), from the Clinical Center of Serbia in Belgrade and from the Clinical Center in Kragujevac in central Serbia.

effect_size.excerpt: According to multivariate logistic regression analysis, there was an association between: frequency of daily urination (OR = 0.18; 95% CI = 0.08-0.39); consumption of liver (OR = 13.81; 95% CI = 2.49-76.69), canned meat (OR = 8.38; 95% CI = 1.74-40.36), fruit juices (OR = 0.08; 95% CI = 0.01-0.56); the highest tertile of pork (OR = 4.55; 95% CI = 1.30-15.93), cabbage (OR = 0.25; 95% CI = 0.06-1.01) and vinegar (OR = 4.41; 95% CI = 1.18-16.50) intake and risk for bladder cancer.

confidence_interval.excerpt: According to multivariate logistic regression analysis, there was an association between: frequency of daily urination (OR = 0.18; 95% CI = 0.08-0.39); consumption of liver (OR = 13.81; 95% CI = 2.49-76.69), canned meat (OR = 8.38; 95% CI = 1.74-40.36), fruit juices (OR = 0.08; 95% CI = 0.01-0.56); the highest tertile of pork (OR = 4.55; 95% CI = 1.30-15.93), cabbage (OR = 0.25; 95% CI = 0.06-1.01) and vinegar (OR = 4.41; 95% CI = 1.18-16.50) intake and risk for bladder cancer.

comparison.excerpt: Consumption of liver, canned meat, pork (h vs l tertile) and vinegar (m vs l tertile) was indicated as a risk factor for bladder cancer

validated_results.title: Dietary soy and increased risk of bladder cancer: a prospective cohort study of men in Shanghai, China.
validated_results.reason: Prospective cohort of Shanghai men reporting adjusted relative risks for dietary soy intake and incident bladder cancer.

extraction.comparison_type: daily soy consumption versus less than once a week
extraction.timing: exposure assessed at baseline interview (1986-1989) before cancer diagnosis
extraction.population: men aged 45-64 years in the Shanghai Cohort Study
extraction.smoking_status: both smokers and non-smokers included; adjusted for cigarette smoking

sample_size.excerpt: Briefly, 18,244 men aged 45-64 years were recruited between January 1986 and September 1989. As of December 31, 2002, 61 incident bladder cancer cases were identified.

cases.excerpt: As of December 31, 2002, 61 incident bladder cancer cases were identified.

effect_size.excerpt: Compared to men consuming soy less than once a week, the RR (95% CI) for those who consumed soy 1-<3 times per week, 3-<7 times a week and daily were 2.05 (0.80-5.29), 2.45 (0.89-6.76) and 4.61 (1.57-13.51), respectively (p for trend = 0.004), after adjustment for age, cigarette smoking and level of education. The soy-bladder cancer risk associations in smokers and non-smokers were comparable.

confidence_interval.excerpt: Compared to men consuming soy less than once a week, the RR (95% CI) for those who consumed soy 1-<3 times per week, 3-<7 times a week and daily were 2.05 (0.80-5.29), 2.45 (0.89-6.76) and 4.61 (1.57-13.51), respectively (p for trend = 0.004), after adjustment for age, cigarette smoking and level of education.

comparison.excerpt: Compared to men consuming soy less than once a week

design.excerpt: we examined the association in a second, geographically distinct prospective cohort of Chinese subjects, the Shanghai Cohort Study

exposure_measurement.excerpt: obtained through in-person interviews at baseline using a food frequency questionnaire
